subject: Humanities
focus: Evaluate neutral eyewitness evidence, then apply the method to survivor testimony in general terms.

source_workbook.basis: Owner brief: LAUNCH Weekly Spring row 42. Workbook not re-read; inherited workbook provenance is retained for traceability only.

assessment_generic: Formative source-method practice and general application. No actual testimony evaluation, archive use or accredited completion inferred.

Supported: Use N1 with N2. Take the six checks one at a time; use the word mat and exact adult reading if helpful.
Compare the boxes and opening time with N3/N4. Point to the link from N1 to N5. Use a frame for a reason and a limit.
Write, type or dictate your own short judgement. Add why survivor testimony matters and one check with one respectful listening action.
Independent: Use all five neutral cards and the six checks. Separate what was seen, planned, recorded later and copied.
Write a short judgement using card codes. Explain one agreement, one difference and why N5 is not an independent check.
Apply the questions to survivor testimony in general terms. Explain purpose, corroboration and respectful listening without inventing an example.
Aspire: Keep the same six checks and common finish. Compare the value and limits of N1 and N4 for a specific claim.
Explain why closer timing or an official-looking record is not a guarantee. State what extra evidence would help and what remains unknown.
Explain why an uncertain detail need not invalidate a whole account. Discuss shared source origins and the limits of missing documents in general terms.

sensitive_response_route: Point to PAUSE or tell the adult quietly. Use the agreed supervised place. You do not need to explain to the group. When ready, choose a private recap or more time with the quiet task. The adult will help you rejoin.
quiet_alternative: Quiet task: put these made-up daily times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 reading; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Then sort pencil and book, cup and plate, by use. No history words or personal story are needed.
staff_care_rules: The school’s chosen memorial-day archive may be used live by the teacher if the school approves. This is optional. The pack names no archive, title, organisation or address. If approved, the teacher previews the exact selection and its context, checks age suitability and the school’s care arrangements, and controls it live. No unplanned browsing or pupil searching. Do not copy, transcribe, paraphrase or add any survivor account to this pack. If school approval, a suitable selection or safe supervision is unavailable, use the complete no-archive route.

The supplied lesson contains no survivor testimony of any kind: no reproduced, paraphrased, invented or composite survivor account. No imagery is supplied or required. Keep any approved live use within the no-imagery, no-graphic-content and dignity rules; if the archive cannot be used safely within them, omit it. The neutral fiction practises source questions only. It does not simulate trauma or make an everyday event equivalent to the Holocaust.

Preview the general discussion privately if helpful. No imagine-you-are tasks, victim roles, historical role play, comparisons of suffering or family-history questions. Do not ask anyone to speak for Jewish people or survivors. No pupil has to share a personal experience or read aloud.

Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, supervising adult, quiet place and private return check before teaching. Keep both pupils supervised. If a sole adult cannot supervise separate spaces, use a calm place in the room or pause the whole group while seeking usual support. Never send a pupil away alone.

If a pupil is distressed, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without sanction or public explanation. Do not probe or insist on a historical recap. Follow existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures and use the usual private recording system.

Interrupt antisemitism calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur; hostility towards Jewish people is unacceptable. Correct the falsehood briefly and follow school procedures. Do not debate Holocaust denial or require pupils to defend victims’ rights. Evaluating a source is not a debate about whether the Holocaust happened.

For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset respectful listening. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid shaming or guessing motives.

Offer the neutral task and a private readiness check. It is not evidence of the history outcome. Record deferred work honestly and offer a later supported return. Record method skills shown on fiction separately from any approved live testimony work; do not claim an archive was used when it was not.
method_context: Historians ask who made an account, when it was recorded and why. They consider what the witness could know, the time since the event and other evidence. They judge what a source is useful for, with clear limits. This pack contains no survivor testimony or imagery.
six_evaluation_checks: Who witnessed the event? Who recorded or edited the account? What could each know?
Keep the event date and recording date separate. How long was the gap?
Why was it made, for whom, and in response to which question?
What is clear, uncertain or outside the witness’s view? Time matters, but later does not mean false.
Compare a specific claim with evidence from a separate origin. Check documents too.
What can this account help us understand? What cannot it establish alone?

source_cards.title: An eyewitness account of a book display
source_cards.label: Invented everyday account only
source_cards.date: Fictional event: 6 October 2026. Account recorded: 20 October 2026.
source_cards.body: I stood by the door as we set out books. I saw three boxes brought to the table. I remember a green cloth. I left before the display opened. I think it opened at ten, but I did not check a clock.
source_cards.link: The fictional witness helped set up the display. The account uses first-person words written by the lesson author. No real person is quoted.
source_cards.think: Which claims concern what the witness saw? Which claim is uncertain or outside their view?

source_cards.title: How the account was recorded
source_cards.label: Invented recording context
source_cards.date: 20 October 2026, fourteen days after the fictional event
source_cards.body: A note-taker asked the volunteer what they remembered about setting up the display. The aim was a short club newsletter. The note-taker wrote the answer down. The volunteer checked the wording. No sound recording is supplied.
source_cards.link: This tells us the maker, recorder, date and purpose within the invented scenario. An account may have more than one person involved in its creation.
source_cards.think: How could the question, purpose and time gap shape what was included?

source_cards.title: A plan made before the display
source_cards.label: Invented planning note
source_cards.body: The display organiser planned four boxes of books, a green cloth and an opening time of 10:00. This note records what was intended. It does not record what actually happened.
source_cards.link: A plan is useful evidence of an aim. It cannot by itself settle a claim about the event.
source_cards.think: Does the plan prove that four boxes arrived or the display opened at ten?

source_cards.title: A setup log made that day
source_cards.label: Invented event record
source_cards.body: A different helper recorded three boxes, a blue cloth and an opening time of 10:05. The helper wrote from their own checks, without using the volunteer’s later account. The helper stayed until the display opened.
source_cards.link: Within the fiction this record has a separate origin and closer timing. It supports some claims and differs on others. A log can still contain an error.
source_cards.think: Which detail agrees with N1? Which details need more checking?

source_cards.title: A later newsletter note
source_cards.label: Invented note based on N1
source_cards.body: The newsletter writer used N1 to describe three boxes and a green cloth. The writer did not attend the display and made no separate check. This note repeats the same account.
source_cards.link: Agreement is not independent confirmation when one source copies another. Trace where a claim came from.
source_cards.think: Are N1 and N5 two separate eyewitness accounts?

source_cards.title: Using the questions with care
source_cards.label: General method guidance only — no survivor account
source_cards.body: Survivor testimony can preserve a person’s voice and perspective. Recordings may support remembrance, education or research. Check the actual purpose and recording context. Historians compare specific claims with documents and other independent evidence. One account cannot tell every person’s story.
source_cards.link: Consider memory and time without assuming a later account is false. A missing document does not by itself disprove an account. Listen without mockery or judging truth by emotion.
source_cards.think: What would you want to know about a recording before using it? How can careful questions and respect work together?

method_checks.scope: Recording context, narrator and interviewer, memory, perspective, ethics and respect. Checked outside the distributable pack; no account text used.

method_checks.kind: Professional guidance for sensitive history teaching
method_checks.scope: Dignity, source context, responsible methods, no victim simulation and no comparisons of suffering. Owner care rules take precedence.

model: N1 is useful for the setup seen from the door. N2 says it was recorded fourteen days later for a newsletter. N4 separately supports the three-box detail. The cloth colour differs, so I would check that claim further. The witness left before opening and was unsure of the time. I cannot use N1 alone to prove the opening time.
success_criteria: Use six source questions on neutral invented evidence.
Compare a claim across records and give a supported judgement with a limit.
Explain the value, checking and respectful use of survivor testimony in general terms.

hinge.question: N1 and N5 both mention a green cloth. N5 used N1. Which judgement fits? A: Two independent witnesses confirm green. B: The same claim has been repeated, so we still need a separate check. C: All eyewitness accounts must be false.
hinge.answer_and_decision_rule: B. N5 depends on N1; it is not independent corroboration. A overcounts evidence and C rejects far too much. Ask both learners privately for a reason. If needed, trace the N1-to-N5 link, then use the parallel question before independent work.
hinge.parallel: N3 planned an opening at 10:00. Does this prove the display opened then? No: it records intention. N4 records 10:05 from a helper who stayed. Check a further independent event record if available; neither a plan nor a log is automatically complete.

pair_work: Evidence Finder locates a claim or question; Question Checker examines maker, timing, purpose and limit. Swap learning roles. No historical role play. Keep each learner’s own response.

evidence.common_finish: In your book, evaluate N1 using the six checks. Use N2 for context and compare N3, N4 and N5. Write a short judgement with two card codes, one supported claim and one limit. Add two general points: why survivor testimony matters and how historians can check it while listening with respect.
evidence.conclusion_frame: N1 is useful for ____ because ____. N2 tells us ____. N4 supports or challenges ____ because ____. N__ cannot prove ____. My careful conclusion is ____. For survivor testimony in general, I would check ____ and listen with respect by ____.

communication: Offer to the Communication portfolio. Record R only after the learner gives an idea, an adult audience replies with one NS (next step), and the learner responds in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Record E only after actual banking. Keep the response mode and actual help. A partner answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.

Words for evaluating accounts
Tuesday 19 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A

Word
Meaning
eyewitness
Someone who was present and saw part of an event.
testimony
An account a person gives about their own experience.
recording context
When, how, why and with whom an account was recorded.
purpose
The reason a source was made.
memory
What a person recalls. Recall is not a recording of every detail.
corroboration
Checking a claim against other evidence.
independent source
Evidence with a separate origin, not copied from the same account.
perspective
What a person could see, know and understand from their position.
limit
What a source cannot tell us or establish on its own.
respect
Treating people and their accounts with dignity while asking careful questions.
Say or point to a word for private help. No reading aloud is required.
A reasoned judgement concerns a particular claim and question. It is not a label of good or bad person.

slides.title: Check an eyewitness account

shapes.name: big-question

Historians ask who made an account, when it was recorded and why. They consider what the witness could know, the time since the event and other evidence. They judge what a source is useful for, with clear limits. This pack contains no survivor testimony or imagery.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: N1: an invented volunteer saw books being set out.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: They left before opening and were unsure of the time.

shapes.name: body-2

Read N1 exactly if needed. Within the fiction, the volunteer saw setup from the door and left before opening. slides.title: Six questions for an account
slides.stage: Introduce the six evaluation questions and scope.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Who made it? When was it recorded? Why was it made?

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: How do memory, time and the witness’s view affect a claim?

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: What can we check? What can it tell us, and what can it not establish?

shapes.name: distinction
shapes.text: Evaluate a specific claim with a reason. Keep the person’s dignity.

slides.notes:
Who: Who witnessed the event? Who recorded or edited the account? What could each know?
When recorded: Keep the event date and recording date separate. How long was the gap?
Purpose: Why was it made, for whom, and in response to which question?
Memory and time: What is clear, uncertain or outside the witness’s view? Time matters, but later does not mean false.
Corroboration: Compare a specific claim with evidence from a separate origin. Check documents too.
Use and limits: What can this account help us understand? What cannot it establish alone?
The question concerns usefulness for a claim, not whether someone is a good or bad person. Different sources may answer different questions. Time affects context but later is not automatically false. No actual survivor example is supplied.

slides.title: A claim with a clear limit
slides.stage: Model N1/N2 with N4; fade the judgement and check both learners.

shapes.name: stage-title
shapes.text: A claim with a clear limit

shapes.name: model-label
shapes.text: Teacher-written model about N1. Every event detail is invented.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: N1: a view from the door. N2: recorded fourteen days later.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: N4 separately supports three boxes. The cloth colour differs.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: N1 cannot prove the opening time: the witness left before it opened.

slides.notes:
N1 is useful for the setup seen from the door. N2 says it was recorded fourteen days later for a newsletter. N4 separately supports the three-box detail. The cloth colour differs, so I would check that claim further. The witness left before opening and was unsure of the time. I cannot use N1 alone to prove the opening time.
Fade the completed judgement; keep N1/N2/N4 visible in print. Ask both learners privately whether N1 proves opening time. No: early departure and expressed uncertainty limit that claim. An exact adult reading is access; a supplied reason is reasoning help. The model is newly authored fiction only.

slides.title: Compare the evidence
slides.stage: Compare N1, N3, N4 and N5; hinge and parallel check.

shapes.name: table-question
shapes.text: Does agreement come from a separate source, or from the same account?

tables: How the same claim was repeated
slides.notes:
Within the invented scenario N4 is a separate record. It supports three boxes; its blue cloth and 10:05 opening differ from N1. N3 intended four boxes, green cloth and 10:00; it cannot prove the result. N5 repeats N1. Do not invent the cause of any difference. The closer log may still err.
N1 and N5 both mention a green cloth. N5 used N1. Which judgement fits? A: Two independent witnesses confirm green. B: The same claim has been repeated, so we still need a separate check. C: All eyewitness accounts must be false.
B. N5 depends on N1; it is not independent corroboration. A overcounts evidence and C rejects far too much. Ask both learners privately for a reason. If needed, trace the N1-to-N5 link, then use the parallel question before independent work.
N3 planned an opening at 10:00. Does this prove the display opened then? No: it records intention. N4 records 10:05 from a helper who stayed. Check a further independent event record if available; neither a plan nor a log is automatically complete.
